net_monthly_income.note: career.net_monthly_income: a net-income figure must declare the circumstances it holds under. Missing: dependents (Number of dependents claimed, or an explicit statement that none are claimed. A household-level median silently averages different household tax positions together.); employee_social_contributions (Whether pension, health and unemployment contributions are deducted from this figure, and which. Some systems have no such deduction; Singapore's CPF is a large deduction that never reaches the worker.); marital_status (Single or married. Usually the largest single adjustment to take-home pay, and a family fact rather than an employment fact.); residency (Resident or non-resident status, where the jurisdiction distinguishes them. Several systems tax residents and non-residents differently.). Defaulting any of these would publish a confident number for a household, tax year or residency status nobody stated.

sources.notes: Route name and duration confirmed from gov.uk rather than memory, as instructed. The official route name is 'Graduate visa' (it replaced the earlier 'Tier 4 Graduate Route'); the current page shows no 'Graduate Route' label, so the 2024-25 restructuring is visible here as a straight rename plus a duration cut. The duration is now date-dependent and this must be modelled as a function of application date, not a single number: 2 years for applications on or before 31 December 2026, dropping to 18 months for applications on or after 1 January 2027, with 3 years reserved for PhD/doctoral completers. A corpus entry that hard-codes '2 years' will be wrong for any applicant applying from 2027 onward. The route cannot be extended; progression to longer stay is via Skilled Worker (see 005).

sources.notes: This is the Immigration Health Surcharge (IHS), the 'healthcare surcharge' referenced by the Student visa page. The Student rate is £776/year, materially lower than the £1,035/year general rate - using the general rate for a student would overstate cost. IMPORTANT for budgeting: a UK Student visa is normally issued longer than the course (gov.uk's own Student visa page confirms up to 1 month before a course over 6 months, and universities note a 4-month post-course tail), so a single 3-year bachelor's course can trigger more than three years of IHS. The fetched page's own worked example (£776 x 2 = £1,552 for a 2-year visa) is the only fully-published worked figure here; totals for a 3-year bachelor course are not printed on this page, so any such total must be computed from the stated rules, not quoted. The pre-2024 history of the rate (£470 for students, £624 general) was seen only in a search-engine snippet of the Immigration (Health Charge) (Amendment) Order 2024, not in a page I successfully fetched - legislation.gov.uk returned an empty body on two attempts (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2015/792/schedule/1) - so the historical rates are deliberately NOT recorded as a claim.

sources.notes: The UK settlement route is officially called 'Indefinite leave to remain' (ILR). The minimum qualifying period on the main work route is 5 years. CRITICAL for a student-corpus: the 5 years is a requirement to 'have lived AND worked in the UK'. Time on a Student visa is not time on a qualifying route, and the Graduate visa is likewise not listed among the qualifying visas on this page. So a student's realistic ILR timeline is 5 years of Skilled Worker, not 5 years total from arrival - a student arriving at 19 would not be eligible before roughly age 24+ and would need to qualify for Skilled Worker in the interim. Supporting figure from the same research pass: Skilled Worker requires a salary of at least £41,700 per year (or the going rate for the job, whichever is higher), so the work route also imposes a substantial earnings bar. Fee recorded: £3,226 per person.
sources.publisher: UK Visas and Immigration (Home Office), GOV.UK

sources.notes: Separate file because the figure comes from a different gov.uk page than the ILR guidance. Recorded because it is the practical bridge between study and settlement: a graduate moving from the Graduate visa to Skilled Worker - the only settlement route named on the ILR page - must clear this earnings bar, and the 'whichever is higher' rule means £41,700 is a floor, not the number most occupations will actually apply. Reduced rates exist and are noted on the same page: 'If you do not meet the usual salary requirements, and you do not work in healthcare or education, you might still be eligible if your salary will be at least £33,400 per year.' Healthcare and education roles use national pay scales instead. Sponsorship is employer-side and mandatory: 'You must have a job offer from an approved UK employer before you apply for a Skilled Worker visa.'

sources.notes: The official name of the requirement, as used by UKVI on this page, is the 'financial requirement' (the page heading reads: Money to support yourself ('financial requirement')). Critical scoping detail confirmed verbatim in the same fetch: the course fee is a SEPARATE test, not part of the maintenance figure - 'You need enough money to pay for your course for 1 academic year (up to 9 months). The amount you need to pay will be on your Confirmation of Acceptance for Studies (CAS).' So the maintenance sums below EXCLUDE tuition, exactly the budgeting trap flagged in the brief. The 9-month multiplier yields 9 x £1,529 = £13,761 (London) and 9 x £1,171 = £10,539 (outside London) for a full 9-month course; those totals are arithmetic on the fetched monthly rates, not separately published figures. Also confirmed: a 'differential evidence requirement' list exists (UK, Australia, Canada, Ireland, New Zealand and ~65 other countries are named on the page) under which applicants may not be asked to prove maintenance funds up front. Source note: the page was fetched 2026-10-05 and shows the current rates; the underlying statutory instrument is the Immigration (Health Charge) / student financial requirement rules, which are revised periodically, so as_of should be read as 'as displayed on 2026-10-05'.
